The October inflation report came out this morning. It is missing the number everyone quotes.

There is no 12-month inflation rate.
Not for food. Not for rent. Not for the overall index.
BLS could not publish one.

Last October, during the funding lapse, nobody went out and collected the prices. You cannot compare this year to a year that was never measured.

My take: the number is gone for a reason that had nothing to do with the economy.

Did you know this year's inflation figure does not exist?

Source: BLS, October 2026 CPI
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Inflation #CPI #Economy

The monthly numbers still exist. Here they are.

Overall prices rose 0.4% in October.
Core, stripping out food and fuel, rose 0.3%.
Shelter rose 0.3%.

September was worse at 0.6%, so the pace eased. Eased is not the same as cheap.

My take: a slower rate of increase still means a higher bill than last month.

Has your weekly shop actually got cheaper?

Source: BLS, October 2026 CPI
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Inflation #CPI #CostOfLiving

Almost every annual figure is missing this month. Three made it through.

Gasoline: up 37.4% over twelve months.
New vehicles: up 0.7%.
Used cars and trucks: down 3.3%.

That is the entire published picture of your year.

My take: fuel is the one place the damage is on the record, and it is the number people feel every week.

What has your fuel bill done this year?

Source: BLS, October 2026 CPI
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Gas #Inflation #CostOfLiving

Food rose faster than everything else last month.

Food overall: up 0.5%.
Groceries: up 0.4%.
Eating out: up 0.5%.

There was nowhere cheaper to move to. Cooking at home rose almost as fast as the restaurant.

My take: when both go up together, the usual advice to just cook more stops working.

Which has gone up more for you — the shop or the takeaway?

Source: BLS, October 2026 CPI
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Groceries #Inflation #FoodPrices

October split the energy bill in two.

Electricity rose 0.9%.
Natural gas fell 0.8%.

Which one you feel depends entirely on how your home is heated — a decision most people never made, they just moved in.

My take: the same month can be a rise or a cut depending on what is in your basement.

Which way did your bill go?

Source: BLS, October 2026 CPI
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Energy #Bills #Inflation

Medical care rose 0.3% in October, after barely moving in September.

Hospital services rose 0.8%.
Physicians' services rose 0.4%.

Hospitals rose nearly three times as fast as the overall index.

My take: this is the line nobody checks until they get the letter.

When did you last look at what your plan actually covers?

Source: BLS, October 2026 CPI
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Healthcare #Inflation #Costs

If prices rise 3% and your pay rises 2%, you took a pay cut.

It just does not look like one on the payslip. The number went up. The number it has to beat went up more.

This is why "I got a raise" and "I am better off" are two different sentences.

My take: compare your raise to prices, never to last year's salary. That is the only comparison that tells the truth.

Did your last raise beat inflation, or just look like it did?

The late fee is the cheapest part.

A payment lands 30 days late.
It goes on your credit file and can sit there seven years.
A lower score raises the rate on the next loan you take.

The fee was $35. The score is what costs you.

My take: autopay the minimum on everything, then pay properly on top. The minimum is insurance, not a plan.

Is every card you own on autopay right now?

Source: FICO scoring factors

#Credit #CreditScore #PersonalFinance

A $5,000 card balance at 22%. The only difference is what you pay each month.

$150 a month clears it in 4 years 4 months and costs $2,798 in interest.
$300 a month clears it in 1 year 9 months and costs $1,022.

Same debt. Same rate. $1,776 difference.

My take: the card company sets the minimum. Everything above it is yours to decide.

Which number is closer to what you pay now?

Source: calculated at 22% APR

$10,000. Nothing added. Thirty years.

Year 10: about $19,700.
Year 20: about $38,700.
Year 30: about $76,100.

The first double takes ten years. The last double takes ten years and adds $38,000.

My take: the boring middle is where it happens, and it is also where most people sell.
